utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good morning. Judge Parker is unable to sit today, so according to the rules, Judge Thelin and I are going to sit today. Mr. Strinovic, good morning. May I remind you of the affirmation you took yesterday, which still applies today. So I will now invite Mr. Domazet to continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all, good morning, Mr. Strinovic. We shall now pick up where we left off. It seems to me we were talking about the way the bodies were exhumed. Were they all packed, as it were, and shipped off to Zagreb on the same day, or depending on the order in which the bodies were arranged? It seems to me you said that this was done when the entire grave was already dug up. Can you please provide some details on this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before in my evidence, the first thing to do was to dug up the entire grave and to get all the bodies exposed, to expose all the bodies in the ground. Then the extraction of the bodies began from top to bottom, from one to 200 bodies were placed in bags individually, photographs were taken of each body, numbers were attached to both bodies and bags. Both were marked and placed in a special container after which the bodies were eventually taken to the forensic pathology institute in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As for these numbers, one to 200, these were applied, as it were, in a chronological order, I assume. How did this work? Body by body or 1, 2, 3, and so on and so forth, or was there no special order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on how readily available, so to speak, the bodies were to be extracted, to be pulled out. The first bodies to emerge from the grave were given the early numbers, so to say. I'm not sure if there was any skipping numbers, just because a body happened to be out of reach at a given point. But the general principle that applied was from top to bottom. And the numbers were applied following the same logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. There may have been minor deviations from this guiding principle, but this is the essential thing. Those in the top-most layers were closer to the first numbers assigned and those bodies that were closer to the bottom of the pit got all the late numbers. I asked you yesterday about the names of the Yugoslav observers, you confirmed that for me. However, I looked at the transcript, and the names were not recorded. Probably because those names are very difficult to transcribe. I'll repeat these names for you and please confirm if these are the right names. Professor, Dr. Dunjic, and professor, doctor, just a minute, please. Dunjic, and professor Dr. Vujadin, Otasevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know these were the experts involved in the exhumation, Professor Otasevic was in Zagreb as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that, you said you remembered him more from Zagreb than Ovcara. You don't actually remember seeing him at Ovcara, but you do from Zagreb. Are you aware of the fact that Professor Otasevic produced a report dated sometime, I think, like November 1996, a report which he invoked during the Ovcara trial in Belgrade. Have you perhaps had an opportunity to see that report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to ask you several things. Please tell me if you agree. You explained the same thing you explained, how the bodies were exhumed, how the bodies were placed in bags. I'm wondering if you were there on this particular day when a CNN crew was allowed inside and were taking footage of the exhumations for the whole day? Were you there on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there myself, but I did hear of something like this happening, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It seems that he was there on that day. He says that the expert opinion, the joint expert opinion of the entire team would be delivered to The Hague Tribunal, which you confirmed. As for any issues related to identification, that sort of information was forwarded to you because you were the experts working on that, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He did speak about DNA analysis being used. There seemed to have been over 50 bodies where there was a hint of identity, but he said that DNA analysis would be nevertheless and that it would be done both in the U.S.A. And in Zagreb. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was talk of there being DNA samples being taken for testing purposes, both in Europe and in the States. I never received any feedback on whether those samples were ever processed and what, if any, the results were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One discrepancy, he talked about 200 bodies, but he believes 199 of those bodies to have been male and one only female. I think your report specifies a figure of two in relation to female bodies. Is this an error that he committed, an oversight, or what do you think this might be?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when Professor Otasevic wrote about the gender of the bodies found. Later sessions of DNA analysis ascertained with a very high degree of certainty that there were two female bodies. It is quite possible that an error occurred during the early stage of the processing, and then this error was perpetuated, resulting in a continuing oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I've just checked, and he wrote the report on the 16th of November, 1996, which I think was just after. Yesterday you said you appeared as an expert at the Belgrade Ovcara trial to give evidence about the exhumation. You remember that, right? Of course you do. On that same day you were there, Dr. Kubat was there, Dr. Milos Tasic, and Dr. Budakov. That was on the same day I think it was the 20th of April last year. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And given the fact that all four of you were there at the same time, the judge asked who first, who now, and as it happened you, as a guest, testified first, and then Dr. Kubat and then Tasic and then Budakov. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Having given evidence, did you remain seated in the courtroom, did you listen to, for example, Dr. Milos Tasic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I gave evidence, Dr. Kubat gave evidence, and then I left the courtroom altogether. And I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you didn't know about these later witnesses, do you perhaps know that Dr. Tasic too had a look at the reports or notes for the autopsies and that he also gave an opinion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, Dr. Tasic's assignment was to look at the reports and to ascertain cause of death in relation to all the bodies found at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'll just ask you something about this, maybe my colleagues will also ask you questions, maybe they will try to clear up individual issues. But I would like to know if you can actually confirm this. Looking at what we have just been speaking about, he says that he found exactly 41 different cases of bodies on which bandages were found, bandages or plaster-casts, with no documentation to indicate any previous injuries underneath those bandages and plaster-casts. You said a lot of things in relation to bodies and which bandages or remains of bandages were found, so could this possibly be the same thing as the cases that you indicated in your tables and documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a special column saying "bandages." And then all the bandages that were found in the report were again mentioned in my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As for his comment concerning cause of death, he says 192 cases of fire-arms, 198 cases fire-arm wounds, and one case of a blunt object trauma. Probably a knife. Does that tally with your own results?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there are any substantial discrepancies. Ascertaining the cause of death is a very complex procedure if you're dealing with bodies that spent a long time in the ground. Maybe there might occur small discrepancies when two different experts give their opinions, but I would say that most of our results did, indeed, tally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to return now to the issue of DNA analysis. You say that Kubat is an expert in this field and I believe he provided testimony, detailed testimony about this at the Belgrade Ovcara trial. I would like to ask you something about the various percentages. I see that science has again been making progress. You spoke about 99.9 per cent, and then you started speaking about 99.999 per cent. So what is this 0.001 per cent that you spoke of as the margin of error? What exactly are we talking about, something that would leave room for the possibility that things weren't what they seemed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, DNA analysis is infallible, to all practical intents. The figure of 99.999 and about six digits, this is not rounded off for purely mathematical reasons. These are added up. In theory, you can never obtain any result that amounts to 100 per cent, so this is the maximum result possible, as it were. As for any errors, obviously errors are always possible. But what this means is that the possibility of an error is practically infinitesimal. If you look at this in real-life terms, in realistic terms, then this would amount to roughly speaking 100 per cent. It is just that we do not choose the figure of 100 per cent to express our degree of certitude, rather we prefer to use 99.999999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is crystal clear. My question: Why wasn't DNA analysis performed on all 200 bodies? Was this because of the lack of reliability that you have just indicated? What about the classic method? You've explained that. Is that method so reliable that there was no need, although, in some cases, DNA analysis was performed, but was there no scientific grounds to do that and was that not in fact part of the initial agreement to do it like that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: DNA analysis first -- was first discovered in 1994, but it was first really applied in 1998 and 1999, it became more of a routine procedure, but it was still relatively new to science and it had not been thoroughly studied yet. On the other hand there was a lot of pressure coming from the families themselves to kick off with the identification procedure. On the other hand, we had a number of cases that were just so obvious to us, so clear cut, that we thought they were in a way cut and dried for us and there was no need to perform DNA analysis and that is why in some cases we decided not to perform DNA analysis. Just one example, the first body identified, the first Ovcara body identified was a man from Zagreb who happened to be in Vukovar at the time. About six months before he went to Vukovar, he had been to his dentist's, where a tooth was extracted, so that a cast was made of both his lower jaw and his upper jaw. The wife, his wife kept this cast and she still had it at home. Therefore when the experts got down to it, when they start trying to identify the body, the wife provided the cast and the mould. And it was very easy to identify the person because this is nearly as reliable as DNA analysis or any other method. There were lots of such cases where incontrovertible evidence was found that seemed rock solid. That seemed as good as any form of DNA analysis or anything else. It is certain on the other hand that the humanitarian aspect was involved too, and pressure coming from the families themselves was one of the reasons accounting for expedited procedure. As time went by, the probability was decreasing that the classic method might be applied successfully in identifying bodies from Ovcara. And the result is that over the last few years you see DNA analysis being applied almost as the sole method.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So despite any success of the classic method, the DNA analysis was still a desirable thing to do, so some families made the request and you tried to meet them, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know whenever a family was still uncertain or whenever they were pressing for DNA analysis, we tried to do our best and keep them happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There is this one case in these documents, the family of Tomislav Baumgertner, 195. The family refused, it seems, to accept identification. Although both the classic method and DNA analysis were applied, however the result was the same and the family refused. Are you familiar with this case and do you know why it was they refused to accept the results?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this wasn't the only case of this happening. There must have been about two or three cases of the family refusing to confirm our results. This, however, is not that unusual, really. Even outside Ovcara it's a fact of life that we encounter in our work. Sometimes families find it very difficult to face these situations. There might even be some rifts within the family, there can be all sorts of reasons for this to be the case, and for a family to refuse to confirm a positive ID. We are simply powerless in cases like these. We do a text-book job, we do the classic method, we do DNA analysis, identity is positive, and we know who the person is. However, despite this, we are still powerless if the family refuses to grant confirmation. And it's impossible to go ahead with the burial. Yet there is nothing we can do about that. These cases are not as rare as people usually imagine them to be. However, in cases like these, as I've already pointed out, we are powerless, and the case officially remains unsolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood properly what you said, does that mean that such a person is still officially missing in that case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all cases that haven't been resolved by the family signing and the people haven't been buried in the ground, are still officially considered as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of the data we received from your testimony and from other evidence it seems that there were at least 11 people who were not identified but up until today only eight of such people remain, meaning that three of those 11 were subsequently identified. One of them is Damir Simenic. I believe that's the number 146. I believe yesterday you said that Marko Ribic for a while was believed to be that person. How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go through the file again, but what I can remember off the top of my head is that there were certain indications that indeed this could be the other person. The family was called in and obviously further processing determined that a mistake was made. I believe the DNA testing was carried out confirming positively who it was. In the initial phases of treatment and gathering data, it is possible that an element carries more weight than the other elements in existence and then we start moving in that direction to confirm that indeed this was one person, but subsequently we find out in our discussions with the family that it is someone else. When this can be confirmed via a DNA test, we do so, and this is nothing unusual in our line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The other two of those who were subsequently identified were Branimir Krunes, number 15, and Josip Mihalec, number 134. Do you know what the reasons were that they were not identified and why did it take so long for them to be identified? Did you come in possession of some other data or perhaps the DNA tests were unavailable at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise because I don't have the documentation before me. But, as I've stated already, problems arise with complicated cases which cannot be resolved in classical terms. Then we go with the DNA analysis. The first issue there is to isolate the DNA from the bones and that can be a very complex thing to do if the remains are old, if the denture is damaged, and then it can take even up to six months to be able to isolate a DNA sample. The next question is how to reach the family to provide us with a blood sample to compare the DNA results with. We have some problems even today, some families cannot be -- get in touch with, and I presume that these two people fell into that category where we had difficulty reaching their families to give us the blood sample to compare that to the results of the DNA test. This is not only a problem with the Ovcara cases, but with some other cases of which we have some 500. They all share the same fate, they haven't been treated with the DNA tests because we simply had no blood samples to compare the results to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, I suppose you have the tables before you, the ones used by Mr. Smith yesterday. Could we please go to tab 1, there is a written report, your written report in the Milosevic case. I believe it was Exhibit 451. Please go to item 21. Perhaps I can read it out. The second sentence is somewhat unclear to me, and I would kindly ask for your comment. It reads as follows: "As the coordinator of the medical team for identification I coordinated the work. However, I neither supervised the work of the identification teams nor examined their reports." Is that what the report reads, and could you please clarify a bit this -- these were your words I quoted, your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And I can clarify. Identifying and processing bodily remains of those killed in wars were carried out by forensic pathologist for all over Croatia, but in some places, such as Zadar, we had an experienced pathologist who had, for 20 years, been doing autopsies and provided testimonies before courts. He wasn't a forensic pathologist per se, but that's precisely what he had been doing for decades. I wanted to use this example to show that we had experienced specialists, experts, who dealt with the exhumations and treatment of those bodily remains. They all submitted their reports, and they were responsible for those. We didn't control their work in the sense of going through the reports and making corrections or additions, but rather such reports remain as they were, and they are available for courts' perusal. They are used in Croatia, as well as by the Tribunal here in The Hague and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but you are talking about the experts who carried out the exhumations or autopsies. Those are the international experts. But it seemed to me that this court referred to the identification teams which were 100 per cent Croatian in their make-up. And I believe you said that you only monitored. As the coordinator, you didn't participate in the very autopsies. Therefore, if I'm not mistaken, this concerns only the identification procedures using the classical method?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I provided the previous answer I did have in mind only the Croatian experts and the job that we did. I have to stress though that 90 per cent of the work was carried out by Croatian physicians, and just a small portion was done by international experts who were chosen by courts and such work was conducted under the control of international organisations and foreign physicians. But I had in mind the cases with Croatian physicians with great experience who did their job as best as they could. My role was to coordinate, meaning that when a mass grave was located, to organise a team, to dispatch it, and to have it present at exhumations. And after that to go on with the treatment of the bodies, be it in situ or in -- in Zagreb or elsewhere. Most of the bodies were treated in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe we agreed yesterday that your report from the Milosevic case does not concern itself only with Ovcara, but with some other things as well. But this is somewhat different, it says I didn't monitor, and I didn't submit the reports. It seems that at least in the Ovcara case your testimony doesn't tally with what is stated here completely.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the work done by the international organisations, I went through the reports that I received. In the case of Ovcara, the forensic institute was given the reports for all 200 bodies that were found at Ovcara. And I received that portion of documentation relating to identification. What we didn't get is the cause of death findings. We went through the documentation in detail, and we used it to identify the bodies subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As regards the identification teams, when the classical method was used, I suppose you, as coordinator, monitored their work and received their reports as well. Am I right to conclude that only Croatian experts participated in that, that there were no international experts or either of the monitors from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the exhumations and examination of the bodies carried out by Croatian experts, as far as I know there were always representatives of international organisations present. In cases when bodies presumably belonging to Serbs were found, then we always had Yugoslav representatives present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I move on, I have a question relating to your testimony in chief. Perhaps you can provide a comment. When Mr. Smith asked you to, you read out an article from Novi Vjesnik of the 28th of October, 1992. The figure mentioned there is 174, and this was prior to the actual exhumations. Since you were a member of the commission for the missing persons, and since you worked at Ovcara, could you comment on that figure, perhaps? Did people mention such a figure before the actual exhumations began? I just want to know the reason why.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say why they used that number. I can't comment any further. In tab 3 in front of you, that's Exhibit 458, we see the table compiled by the international experts. There are 56 cases there of tentative identification suggested in the last column. Could we see that as their proposal later on checked and verified by your team, which in turn resulted in the final figure of 83 as regards tentative identifications?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The initial information as regards identities was received by the international expert. They thought these indeed could be the names associated with the names shown here, and there were 56 such cases, but we had to run our check on that, and verify. But this is the group that you are concerned with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the table there is a date to be seen. Is that the date of exhumation or the date of autopsy, or perhaps something else?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are probably asking me about the first date mentioned. I am uncertain about the date. This is probably the date when the exhumation was carried out in September of 1996. One can presume that that was the date when the bodies were being extracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If that is so, could we agree that there is -- that there are very different dates shown. If these indeed are the dates of the exhumations, does that mean that those bodies were exhumed over a number of days and not in a single day?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if these are the dates of exhumations, then obviously they vary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please look at tab 5? That's Exhibit 459, the list of the missing persons. And there are still those 11 unidentified ones, meaning that that was before the three were identified subsequently. At the end there is an attachment of six names with a note. It reads, "Z-N/A." Have you found that? Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't know. I didn't put this table together, but someone from the office for the detained and missing persons would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go further down there are 76 names. Who are those people? Is that the list you mentioned of potentially missing, since those names do not appear in any list of those who were identified?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the list that follows the 200 people from Ovcara are those who went missing from the Vukovar Hospital. They were on one of the lists, the one which had around 270 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If we add those figures up, we would come with a total of 270 or 280. Perhaps that would be the very list you've mentioned. You mentioned that list in one of my initial questions as the figure that was at the disposal of the commission, and you said that the numbers varied and that some estimates were even far higher. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Given the fact that you became a member of the commission late in 1991, and the commission was not only dealing with Ovcara but with other mass graves, and potential mass grave sites as well, did your commission take part in any way in something that happened in Gospic around this time of the year, back in 1991, with Serb civilians as the victims? Zoran Stankovic, a person you spoke about yesterday, was in some way involved there. So my question, were you personally or any members of your team involved in the identification procedure in Gospic? So my question, were you personally or any members of your team involved in the identification procedure in Gospic.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that specific case, the Gospic case, when Dr. Stankovic was there, there was a team from Rijeka, the chief forensic pathologist from Rijeka working jointly with Dr. Stankovic. But as far as I know, no one from our commission was actually present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, when I speak about the commission, I mean the one of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commission for detained and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You remember, Mr. Strinovic, Mr. Smith asking you yesterday about some names from these lists. He wanted to have some of the names compared for errors, for spelling mistakes. And you told us a little about that. And you think those were simple errors, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we first of all agree that the name of Josip is perfectly common in Croatia, but there is also another variant, as it were, Josif, J-o-s-i-f, as opposed to Josip with a P. Can you confirm that these are two different variants, if you like, of the same name?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is possible. However, in Croatia Josip is far more common. Josif is extremely uncommon on the other hand. I don't actually know anyone named that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the registrar please put 462 on the ELMO, Exhibit 462, that's tab 7. The 65 ter number is 881, both English and B/C/S ERN 00560699. This isn't the number, 00560699.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is a photocopy, if you look at your own tabs perhaps you can find these IDs. The ID of Mr. Balog. I would love to have that on the screen, though. What we see now is an autopsy report. Yes, that's it. If we could please just zoom in a little. We talked about him yesterday. You remember, don't you? We could please zoom in slightly, since it's very small and difficult to see. Do you have that on your screen, Doctor? Would I be right in stating that his name, as reflected on his ID, based on which he was identified, and we just cannot be wrong, is J-o-s-i-f, with an F. Please don't just nod. For the sake of the record, speak up.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. His ID says "Josif."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But we've seen a lot of these tables giving his name as Josip, with a P. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. It is quite obvious that whoever was entering all the names was not familiar with this other variant of the name, Josif, which was quite uncommon, so the person just assumed that the name was Josip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. You have pointed out the name is a bit uncommon, but this may be a simple error, such as those you discussed yesterday. This can only be Josif Balog. Certainly not Josip, although the names do indeed sound alike. I hope we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Could these be two different persons, just because of this one letter discrepancy? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the reason is what I've just stated for you. That and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This does follow from your answer, sir, but I presume this to be a mere assumption on your part, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Strinovic. I have no further questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing for the transcript. I don't think the last answer was reflected. The witness said "yes," when I asked him whether this was a mere assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strinovic my name is Mira Tapuskovic. I am one of Miroslav Radic's Defence counsel. I hope you can hear me clearly enough, since we have some problems with our microphones. You mentioned several times yesterday about you going to Hungary, especially in 1992, whether Pecs or Budapest. Do you remember the meeting you had with the International Red Cross people, and the commission of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that took place on the 12th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I remember the date. I remember the -- I remember meetings, there were several of those. It's really difficult for me to say now who was when and where, who attended a particular meeting or what specifically was discussed at each of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. But do you remember that at one of these meetings Dr. Vesna Bosanac was with you as a member of the Croatian delegation? She was the hospital director when the civilians and patients from the hospital were evacuated back in 1991? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. She was there. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if, on that occasion, Vesna Bosanac gave you a list of persons who allegedly had gone missing from the Vukovar Hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know if she did or not. But there was no need for her to do that in Pecs or in Budapest. She could easily have done this in Zagreb, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question was if on that particular occasion a list was given to you. She came with you to this meeting in Budapest and my conclusion is, since she was not a member of the commission, or at least that's not what our information indicates, her role was probably to speak about those persons who had allegedly gone missing from the Vukovar Hospital. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that probably was the reason she attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about any time later on during the identification procedure. What about Vesna Bosanac or anybody else on her behalf from Croatian's health ministry giving you a list of persons who had allegedly gone missing from the Vukovar Hospital with accompanying information?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never received such lists. As far as I know, these were forwarded to the commission. And later on, when the examinations started, the lists were used to identify bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you personally never received any such lists from Vesna Bosanac or anyone else on her behalf. However, such lists were handed over to your commission, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The exhumation took some time, the autopsies took some time, we know about the time-line because this is something that you shared with us yesterday. You told us how long this had taken. Identification is the lengthiest procedure of all, we might say. What about the Croatian laws? Do the Croatian laws say anything about any dead-line for submitting a request or a questionnaire to ascertain whether a person was detained or missing? Are there any laws in the Republic of Croatia specifying a dead-line on how long persons can be registered as missing and how long this question mark over their fate is allowed to remain in place?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say. My job is the identification procedure. I'm not sure how long the procedure can take under the existing laws, but I know that every effort will be made to identify any bodies. I think that is open-ended and there is no specific dead-line for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think your answer is in reference to the identification procedure. Perhaps the question was a little too long, or rather there were two questions instead of just one. After 1995 is it possible to fill in forms or questionnaires in order to inform your commission or the Croatian government about the fact that families or relatives were looking for someone who had gone missing in Croatian territory back in 1991 during the war?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask someone else. You'll have to ask someone whose job that happens to be. This is certainly not a question for a forensic pathologist, and the question then follows from -- the answer then follows from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you remember that visit to Budapest with Vesna Bosanac. Do you perhaps remember how many persons she reported as missing from the Vukovar Hospital? What about the figure of 236 persons? Is this something she might have provided at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember the exact figure. This strikes me as a distinct possibility what you have just suggested, but the simple truth of the matter is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You testified in the Milosevic case back in March 2003. For the benefit of my learned friends, the page number is 17938, lines 8 and 9. You state here that 255 persons from the Vukovar Hospital were reported as missing to your commission. I assume that your answer would have been accurate at the time, wouldn't it. Can you tell me what you base this figure on, what documents, what information, when you spoke of these 255 missing persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember now, I think this was something that I got from the office for detained and missing persons. They had the documents, they gave me this figure. It's not something I heard at one of the meetings. I was provided with this specific figure before my testimony back in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please don't hold it against me if I use the terms "commission" and "office" interchangeably. You yourself pointed out the roles were changed a while later, although the essential tasks remained the same. You mentioned Dr. Clyde Snow yesterday who was in charge of the exhumation to all practical intents, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that isn't true, he want in charge of the exhumation. Clyde Snow was the first person to discover the site. He was there twice in 1992. The entire exhumation was led by international experts, but Clyde Snow was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know that in September 1992 Clyde Snow was in Zagreb at the medical faculty, in fact, where he met Dr. Kostovic? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think the date you have just specified is exact, and I did know about their meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Clyde Snow testified in the Dokmanovic case back in 1998 on the 17th of March, to be more specific. The page is 1520, lines 18 and 19. Dr. Snow said that Dr. Kostovic had informed him about the fact that 200 persons were reported as missing from the Vukovar Hospital. Are you familiar with this bit of information? Is this something that Dr. Kostovic at one time or another shared with you, or perhaps this is a figure that you heard from Dr. Snow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the specific figure. Can't say I heard about that. I did know that Dr. Kostovic had a figure that he was using at the time, but this normally varied, and the range was pretty wide, from 200 to 400. I do not know what it was that Dr. Snow said specifically, which figure he was using, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you will agree with me, won't you, that for all these years I've just given you the first figure bandied about by Vesna Bosanac in July 1992 during that meeting in Budapest. And then the trials at this Tribunal, over this time we have seen a wide range of figures being used in relation to the persons who had allegedly gone missing from the Vukovar Hospital. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was exceedingly difficult to have a reliable list of persons missing from the Vukovar Hospital. A lot of people were just passing through, there was a lot of coming and going, and this may have caused some of the discrepancies and aberrations in these figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I asked you about you compiling different lists of missing persons, those who had allegedly gone missing from the hospital. Mr. Domazet referred to your testimony in the Belgrade case, the case that we colloquially refer to here as the Belgrade Ovcara case. You testified before that court on the 20th of April, 2005. For the benefit of my learned friends from the OTP, the page is 3, transcript page is 3, number 3. You say you first compiled lists of missing persons from the hospital. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what exactly you meant when you said, "I compiled lists." Or rather, "We compiled lists." We have this reference in the plural on several different occasions. "We have lists of missing persons from the Vukovar Hospital." What exactly do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about gathering information in order to compile a list of missing persons, what I meant was the commission for detained and missing persons did this job. The commission gathered all the information and compiled the lists. As a forensic pathologist, all I wanted from the lists was to retrieve as much antemortem information as possible. I wanted to use the most comprehensive list of people missing from the hospital in order to obtain as many names as possible, and then I could go back to any remaining families and get more information. This was about gathering solid, rock-hard antemortem information based on any lists compiled by the commission at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it seems that the sheer quantity of antemortem information that you were able to gather was what really mattered to both you and the commission. The exact figure of missing persons was not as material, was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing is, no one on earth was able to ascertain the exact figure. This was always a ball-park figure being used. I understand you would like to know the exact figure, but back then it was simply impossible to ascertain that figure. You had to cast net as wide as possible, you had to gather as much information as possible, so as to make your job easier later on, make your own job easier. So that the identification procedure might be easier later on, perhaps. So the idea was to cast the net as wide as possible in search of information, any information in relation to those missing from the hospital and the guiding principle was, yes, gather as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Precisely because of what is stated in the transcript from that trial, the plural is mentioned, several lists. Do you remember the exact number of those lists?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. The only thing I know is that the figure that appeared was around 400, and that's when we attempted to collect the antemortem data.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please refer to the set of documents given to you yesterday by the OTP where the tab numbers are. Please go to tab 1, that is Exhibit 451. This is your report, Mr. Strinovic. I don't see the date on the report, but I presume it was compiled for the OTP in the case against Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you testified in March, I presume you wrote this in early 2003?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that should be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go to para 21 and 22 of your report. My learned friend, Mr. Domazet, asked you a question concerning paragraph 21. I won't dwell on its contents, but rather on the titles. When one reads your report one can see that the titles of individual paragraphs are formulated as questions, they begin with, "Did you ..." or at least this particular one does. All of those 22 questions were put to you by the OTP asking you to provide answers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go back to paragraph 10 of your report on page 2, I will read out, and perhaps you can confirm whether I've read it out correctly. [In English] "I must emphasise that primarily forensic pathologists were used to do the work." [Interpretation] Have I read that portion correctly, the first part of the first sentence in paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the original I stated that primarily forensic pathologist were used to do the work.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained the difference between an anthropologist, a pathologist, and a forensic pathologist. And you also spoke about the way teams were formed. You said that you insisted that each team be given a forensic pathologist and an assistant. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When reading paragraph 10 one can see that you mostly used pathologists, experts who deal with disease, first and foremost, rather than using forensic pathologists who deal with violent deaths, as explained by yourself yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it must be a mistranslation. In Croatian it clearly stated what I said yesterday, that primarily we used forensic pathologists and only exceptionally when they were not present we made use of pathologists. I said that loud and clear yesterday, and I believe it has been written down that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I wanted to discuss this paragraph with you, because obviously there was a mistranslation. In the original we have forensic pathologists, and in the English it just says "pathologists."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify further. Often in the English language the term pathologist can also include forensic pathologists. But in the Croatian language we have clearly separated to two specialisations, that of pathologist and that of forensic pathologist. They are completely separate, whereas in English the border is not so clear. Pathologists can do either of the things, and I presume that was the reason for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with those differences at a later stage of cross-examination when we start talking about the exhumations, identifications, and the use of international teams. You have mentioned the Zadar case where in one of your teams you said you had an expert without proper forensic pathologist papers, diplomas. Was that Mr. Josip Dujela?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've discussed his work in Martic case two months ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm to us that when identifying the 200 bodies from Ovcara there was always a member of the team who had all the proper qualifications for that work, or rather to clarify, did you always have a forensic pathologist on board? Or were there cases of physicians doing that work such as with Mr. Josip Dujela from Zadar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the work of the international experts is concerned at Ovcara, I never inquired about their qualifications. I always believed that those who sent them there chose the right people. It wasn't my job to control their expert knowledge and qualifications. The only thing I know was that there were radiologists, dental experts and anthropologists there from the international community, as well as forensic pathologists. As to pathologists being there, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Strinovic. On line 25, page 27 my question was precisely so, I asked you about the identifications only. Yesterday you said you were the person who put those teams together. Once the autopsies were carried out, the international teams who did that turned the bodies over to your commission. Is that your statement from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. When it comes to identifications, that is extracting the elements from the documentation necessary to compare with the antemortem data, that part of work was carried out by the forensic institute in Zagreb. I was there, as well as my other colleagues, forensic pathologists. We worked on that to conclude the identifications. We only used forensic pathologists from Zagreb as concerns identifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely what I wanted to ask you. In your work concerning the mortal remains of the 200 people from Ovcara were you able to meet Dr. Yvonne Milewski in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of delegations and people who came to the institute concerning Ovcara and similar cases. And I must admit that that name doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can refresh your memory. Dr. Yvonne Milewski worked on the autopsies. We have her report, and she carried out about 11 per cent of all the autopsies. She even stated that in a way she coordinated the work of the other pathologists there. Therefore, she was routinely present during autopsies, and that procedure took a couple of months, longer than the exhumation itself. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room where we did autopsies there were constantly 30 to 40 people present. Of course some of them introduced themselves, but then I really can't remember this lady.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Milewski was asked by the OTP to give evidence. She put together a separate report. Her report and her evidence was part of this case. I refer to Exhibit 381.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have a break now, please, so that I can go through my questions and perhaps shorten my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tapuskovic. We will have a break of 20 minutes now. So we will resume at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We may continue, Mr. Strinovic. We will deal with the tables in your report. I presume you would agree with me that this report you prepared for the OTP in the case against Milosevic contains several tables and they pertain to various locations in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please go to the first table. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your report that is the table entitled, "Totals." The ERN number in the English is 0307-1 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interprets didn't catch the last two figures. 98.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that this table reflects the total number of victims examined by your office, by yourself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I will interrupt my series of questions for a moment. During the break I was told that on page 29, lines 14 and 15, when I asked the witness about Dr. Yvonne Milewski, and when I stated that she was under a contract with this Tribunal, that hasn't been entered in the transcript. She was contracted by the Tribunal, and that report has already been given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, to go back to the table, Mr. Strinovic, sorry for interrupting. In the third column, actually in the third row, it states "Zagreb Ovcara" meaning that the examination or the treatment of the mortal remains was carried out in Zagreb. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There are three types of columns that is under different headings. One reads "established," the other group is "probable," the third one being "unknown." These headings, do they pertain to the cause of death, because there's no clear explanation of what "established", "probable," and "unknown" means. Is that regarding the cause of death or the total number of mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That pertains to the cause of death, established, probable, and unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in the column just below "established" we have "shooting," meaning the cause of death, as you stated, was shooting from a fire-arm. If we go three rows down we see the figure of 200.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All other columns are empty. There are no entries, and in the far right column we have the total of 200. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So according to this part of the table there were 200 cases at Ovcara, 200 cases of shootings as the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we could read that table, although I need to say that I don't know when this table was put together, particularly in relation to all the data we received regarding the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the break you confirmed that you compiled this report for the OTP just before your testimony in the Milosevic case, and this was in March 2003, wasn't it? Would you agree with me that the table was compiled just before March 2003?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this particular table. I don't know when exactly it was compiled. If I look all this information, the information was obviously obtained from the Office for Detained and Missing Persons. Therefore, I really can't say when the specific table was actually produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the table is an integral part of your report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There are all together about 10 of these tables, and just one of these, the one that is on page 7, the ERN in English is 0307-1920. Have you got that table, sir? Perhaps if I could help you with this, the heading is "Ovcara." For the interpreters, this is table number 1. I see that Mr. Strinovic is finding it difficult to find that one, since in this folder we have both the B/C/S and the English. I know there's been some confusion about the page numbers, and that may be why Dr. Strinovic is taking a long time. The heading is "Ovcara." I think you have it in front of you right now. That must be the one. And it's on our screens too. Mr. Strinovic, do you agree with me that there's only one table in reference to the mortal remains found at Ovcara, only one such table in your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the upper left corner of the table there is the letter N, equals, 200. Would I be right in concluding based on that N stands for "number", and that the total is 200, would that be a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further, "cause of death," "gunshot injuries", or rather, "fire-arm injuries"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could now please move to tab 4. This is Exhibit 457. Mr. Strinovic, this is a separate table, and it is not part of your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the report that we discussed a while ago at tab 1. The report that you used for your testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it's not part of that report, is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may put it that way, we have a heading here which says "paragraph 49." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 49, is that the number of the Croatian indictment against Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday. During your evidence in chief you were asked about this table, and you said that you and your associates compiled this table with information with cause of death information which you obtained sometime in 2002 or thereabouts. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is probably true.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For your information, I've compared the Croatian indictment against Slobodan Milosevic, and paragraph 49 only mentions the alleged victims from the Vukovar Hospital. If we look at this table we see that in 195 cases the cause of death was established. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of those 195 cases, in 188 cases the death was caused by gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I gave a different figure, but I think the right figure is 188.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I mean. Can you please explain this? This table was compiled for the purposes of the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic. You said you compiled this with your associates. You say that the figure of 188 is in reference to the number of deaths caused by gunshot wounds. A while ago we discussed the table from your report, the one with the heading, "Ovcara," and the one with the heading "total," in which you mention a total of 200. 200 deaths caused by gunshot wounds. Can you please explain how this is possible? How is it possible within such a short space of time, for such different information to be provided in a document that you submit to an international institution such as the Tribunal, regardless of the case in question?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just by looking at it, it seems quite obvious to me that in the first case we had less information about those 200 persons who died as a result of gunshot wounds, who were shot. Later on we were given more accurate, more detailed information, it was based on this later set of data that we had that we compiled this second report. The information provided was better quality, it's as simple as that. We did not look at the cause of death. We tried to use some documents and reports or partial reports to arrive at certain conclusions. The first bit of information about 200 people who were shot died as a result of gunshot wounds, was the result of our information at the time. Later on we realised, based on information that we received later on, that the figure of 195, 188 of those were accounted for by gunshot wounds. So it's obvious that there were two different kinds of information being provided, and this applies to both the first time around and second time around. We did not have information of our own, this was information submitted to us, and as information was submitted to us, we tried to improve the accuracy of our reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I've heard your explanation, but we do agree that your report does not bear a date, and we ascertained in a round about way as it were when it was your report was produced. You confirmed that it was compiled early in 2003. What about this table, there is no date on it, is there? But we have concluded that it was made for the purposes of the Croatian indictment against Slobodan Milosevic which was raised, I'm not mentioning the date, but certainly it was after 2000 [Realtime transcript read in error "2003"]. You say you had no information, you say you received information from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is an error about the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic. The Croatian indictment, it says 2003, I was using a ball-park figure of after 2000. At this point in time I'm not interested in the exact year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say you received information from some other source. It wasn't generated by you, in other words. When were the autopsies finished, and when did you receive all the documents, the entire documentation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, the identification documents were submitted to us immediately after we finished our job in late 1996 and early 1997. These were parts of the autopsy reports that had to do with identifying bodies, but not with cause of death. We never received entire reports, we always received bits of reports that we could use to draw certain conclusions, but cause of death reports were never part of what we received. We used whatever information we received, and this is clearly reflected. But one thing that I have to point out is that this was not submitted to the Croatian side through any legal channels. I'm not sure how I acquired those eventually, whether it was here at the Tribunal or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, I remember exactly what you said yesterday. What you said about how you acquired some parts of the documentation, and you even indicated clearly the specific portions of the autopsy reports which you received. However, you received all those data at a point in time when the autopsies had been long over. When you eventually compiled these reports, had you by this time received any other kind of information except for information related to the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what other type of information we possibly could have received. Those who performed the autopsies submitted reports to us and those were final reports, not containing the cause-of-death section. That was not disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that all these three tables, the total table, the Ovcara table and the paragraph 49 table were compiled based on the same set of documents, on the same pool of information, to put it that way, that your office was in possession of?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously not, otherwise the tables would be identical. We had different documents, and that's why the information in these tables are different. In one of the tables you have 200 persons killed as a result of gunshot wounds and in the other table you have different figures, 198. If we had been using the same information all the time, our results would have tallied. That much is obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I asked you a while ago, whether there was additional information later on, and you clearly said none. Let us move on, however. I'm still looking at paragraph 49, we still have that in our screens. In the lower left corner, it reads, "age range 16 to 72." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the table says, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We shall in due course be discussing the report of Dr. Yvonne Milewski. You say you don't know her. What would be your answer if I suggested to you that Dr. Milewski, who looked at all 200 autopsy reports pursuant to a request by the OTP, concluded that the age range of the victims was 17 to 66?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this study was conducted, which year. But we looked at our reports when we were identifying bodies, and this is the range that we established. The two ends of the range signify obviously the youngest person found and the oldest person found at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that the discrepancy between 72 and 66 appears to be six years? This is a considerable figure, when ascertaining the age of dead bodies that were found somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat this. I have no idea what this study was based on, whether there doctor based her findings on anthropologists' findings, or on death certificates. Thus knowing the date of birth in relation to each and every body. We did this based on death certificates, which means that we were in possession of such information as to indicate when all of these people were born.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We are now looking at this table, and we all received a set of documents yesterday. Can we please have on our screens Exhibit 381. This is Dr. Milewski's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to remind you, the report and the transcript were admitted under Rule 92 bis some 10 days ago or so. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me what basis that Dr. Milewski have for her work, and I said that she was contracted by the OTP to compile the report. In its introduction entitled, "The Analysis of Pathological Findings During Autopsies of Bodies Exhumed from the Ovcara Site Close to Vukovar in Croatia on the 4th of March 1998." She indicates her confirmation that she checked 200 autopsy findings. Therefore, Dr. Milewski went through the same documents and the same autopsy findings you had at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It seems I need to clarify yet again. These are two different things. Dr. Milewski had autopsy reports before her in which the given forensic pathologist or anthropologist provided approximate age determined at autopsy. That's what she based her report on. We compiled our report based on the identified persons. The anthropologist cannot provide the exact year of birth, but rather their margin of error is plus or minus five years. Based on the death certificate we determined the exact of date of birth, once the person had been identified. That's why we used precise information, and the doctor used information, approximate information, based on the findings. We did have the same documentation at our disposal, but she used the findings. Among other entries when it states age, we have a range. After the identification we were in possession of the exact date of birth, and as such they were entered and that's the basis of what we put down between the ages of 16 and 72. And these are two completely different things. We can't compare that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The age range does contain a certain margin of error for various reasons but once the entire identification process has been completed we can be certain of the given person's age. To move on to a different topic dealt by -- dealt with by Dr. Milewski, and I need to clarify my position here. You came here as an OTP witness, and Dr. Milewski provided her finding and report upon OTP's request. And her report and her tables, as well as her evidence, was admitted into the file. Could you now please go to the table I termed paragraph 49? That is in tab 4. I would kindly ask the usher, what we have now is Dr. Milewski's statement, and right after comes her report, the sixth page in the English, paragraph E. I will go on with my questions while we're waiting for the document. In your table entitled "paragraph 49," it reads that in four cases the cause of death is unknown. Is that correct? In 188 cases the cause of death was shooting. And provided we will be able to locate the page, that's page 6, not of the statement but of the report. Exhibit 381. We have it on the screen. According to our data, both the statement and the report by Dr. Milewski were given one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we seem to be unable to have the document. This is the statement. It's not the document I had in mind. With Your Honour's leave, I have the B/C/S version of the report here, and perhaps the usher could assist me in handing it over to the witness so that the witness could read it for himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, on that page that you have in front of you the several lines at the bottom are marked in orange. That is paragraph E.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out paragraph E?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph E states: "There are seven individuals in which a cause of death could not be reached with objectivity or with certainty."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Milewski provided her findings in 1998. And you compiled your tables, especially the paragraph 49 table, somewhat later. What one can read there is that in four cases the cause of death could not be ascertained. Could you provide a scientific explanation for the discrepancy between these two separate findings as regards the number of those cases in which the figures differ concerning the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can provide a brief or an extended explanation from various points of view. What is of essence here is that we did not have the entire documentation at any given time. When we compiled this table we were given the cause of death as were given to us in the documents we received. I must state that it is difficult to determine the exact cause of death in such cases. Therefore, the autopsy experts in the Ovcara cases could come up with various explanations. Therefore, the cause of death as entered could not have been the single solution possible. There may have been interpretation of their findings. If we gave this report and the documentations to various forensic pathologists, I'm pretty certain that they would come up with different figures too. Because the cause of death column is not a solid one, but rather a diversified one. The cause of death can be somewhat different as regards to shooting or trauma. Perhaps the best solution would be to assess each case individually regarding the injuries that exist and the injuries can be analysed in different ways. And then we could establish a more or less certain diagnosis as to the cause of death. In cases such as these, when some time as passed, there are numerous changes. First of all, there are changes to the clothing. You can see the holes in the clothes but with time they disappear. We can also see the defect on the skin, but the skin disintegrates. Then we go further down to the organs, but they can disintegrate too. Then we reach the bones. Some bones have neat fractures which do not correspond to bullet injuries, but some bones fall apart in such a way that it is difficult to conclude what the actual cause was. I'm trying to explain to the Chamber and to you why this category of the cause of death is a complex one. It is difficult to come up with a certain figure out of the great number of cases. We had data we received with the causes of death stated, and on the basis of that we put together this paragraph 49 table. If we were to analyse these cases again it would be difficult to come up with the exact figure. You are talking about small shades, nuances, and even top experts could offer different interpretations. It is easy to establish the type of injury in a person who has passed away recently, but if we are talking about six or more years, the situation changes completely. And even the bodies at Ovcara differed. Those that were closer to the surface were poorly preserved, whereas those at the bottom were better preserved because more soft tissue remained. Therefore, we could see the actual injuries. So, to reiterate, there is a difference between four and seven, but I tried to account for that. It concerns the interpretation, the way we read documentation. And apart from that, we have received a list of causes of death from which we could establish the exact figures. Therefore, that list was used to make this table, although we didn't make the initial list concerning the cause of death. We had the previous table with that 200, and now we have this one with a number which is somewhat less. I am trying to explain to the Chamber that it is a very delicate issue, and as I have stated, discrepancy may occur. But this margin of error between four and seven, is a very small one.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You've also provided an answer to one of my future questions. I won't go through all details of Dr. Milewski's report, but I believe we can conclude that because of the very reasons you have cited now there was a difference between the total number of those who passed away because of gunshot injuries, and the number appearing in your table, which is 188, and the table called "paragraph 49," and the figure offered by Dr. Milewski. She stated that gunshot injuries were the cause of death in 190 cases. Therefore, the same reasons could account for that discrepancy as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you are trying to tell us that various experts of same qualifications of the same specialisation using the same material can come up with different findings.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The degree of certitude differs as to the cause of death. And, as such, it can be interpreted in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've testified in the Belgrade Ovcara case, and upon the court's requests there were experts who testified there as well. You've mentioned them by name. Their results, as regards certain parameters, differ from your results as well as from the results provided by Dr. Milewski. Therefore, I believe the same explanation can be used in that instance as well.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the reports of my colleagues from Novi Sad, but I am almost positive that we could explain the discrepancies by using the same explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to reorganise my questions yet again, since you've already answered some of them. Since we are talking about autopsies and establishing cause of death, in this specific case of the bodies from Ovcara you were not the person who actually carried out the autopsies. But nevertheless I believe you can provide an answer to my next question. When you testified in the case against Milan Martic in April of 2006, there was discussion of the testimony of Mirko Blazanovic [phoen] or Blazanovic from Lipovacka Dreznica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the late Mirko Blazanovic died of neck injuries or soft tissue injuries, and this is what you took into account when you made that assertion. After the post mortem was carried out, and your testimony on this matter is in the transcript of the 12th and 13th of April, 2006, and it says that regardless of the fact that the remains of Mr. Blazanovic were examined, the exact cause of death could not be determined as a gunshot wound and that witness testimony was taken as true that he had sustained neck injuries and then it was noted that in the case of this victim, that he -- the cause of death was a gunshot wound. Can you please tell me whether this approach of establishing the cause of death by examining the documents that you had could have been and was applied in any case or in relation to any remains from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what those who wrote out the causes of death were guided by. As far as I know, exclusively on the level of the -- on the basis of the findings and radiological findings, it could have been established whether there were in any projectiles or particles that could suggest a cause of death. And based on other post-mortem findings, the cause death were established.
