As far as I know they did not use any other information or elements to decide what the cause of death was, but they only used the information they obtained during the post mortem.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you did not answer my question. You testified in a different case that you were familiar with a case that a victim was reportedly killed by fire-arms even though this was something that was not established in a post mortem. So my question is, are you aware, I'm not asking about whether your teams from your commission worked that way. What I'm asking you is if you know whether this approach of establishing the cause of death was applied in relation to any of the remains from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I did answer, that I am not aware of any such case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you rule out 100 per cent that there were no such cases?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not because I was not the one who wrote the protocol or the one who entered the information about the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a lot, Doctor, about the procedure from the discovery of the grave site, then the identification process, and we can agree that practically there were three phases in this whole matter; the exhumation phase which took about 40 odd days, then the autopsy phase, which took three months, and then the stage of identification, which practically, according to what you told us, is still not finished today?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And nobody knows when that stage would be completed, the stage of identification. According to what you told us yesterday and today, we can agree, perhaps, that none of the Croatian experts or doctors, medical specialists in the teams that you formed, as far as I understood, and that you coordinated, did not sign a single document relating to establishing the cause of death or the post mortem. This was something that was entirely done by international experts?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, that is how this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that in the initial years until the discovery of the grave site, or actually -- or rather that you said that this took until 1995, that the primary objective of the commission was to compile as much information as possible, to hold meetings in order to compile as much information of antemortem information as possible, that would serve as the basis for the identification process which you knew would eventually take place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated, and I think that this was in the Belgrade Ovcara case, and yesterday you told us here that in 80 per cent of the cases the identification was conducted by the classic method on the basis of information received from relatives, friends, neighbours or anyone who was able to provide relevant information, and that the rest of the identified remains were identified by DNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not exclusively applied to Ovcara, but for all the cases processed by us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So all the identifications conducted on the territory of Croatia, as well as all the remains of victims that were killed in the time period during the conflicts in Croatia, that's the period it applies to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, now, if we look at tab 6, that is Exhibit 460. We see the table. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the table was drafted in 2006. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that it was drafted in the forensic medicine institute, and that you worked on it with your colleagues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A break-down is given here, and of the 200 total remains, it is noted how many of them were identified by the classic methods and how many were identified using DNA, and then you have the identified -- identifying Ovcara numbers of the remains, in which case the identity was not established for those remains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the last page of that table you provided the total data, and there it states that out of a total of 200 remains, 192 were identified, and that of that 93 were identified with the classic method and 99 using the DNA method. Is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have to just note that for the transcript. If we look at the figures and the ratio of 93 identities established by the classic method and 99 cases using DNA analysis we see that the ratio is not 80:20?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Actually the ratio here is 1:1, practically. Can you please explain why this is so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. This was the largest mass grave exhumed in Croatia, and at the start of the identification process all the persons were identified using the classic method. These were very clear cases with a lot of elements, and which were so convincing that it was possible to carry out an identification acceptable to the relatives. So during the first year identification was done by the classic method; DNA as a method was not so perfected at that time. As time went on and the remaining cases became more and more complicated it was not possible to get enough elements using the classic method, so then we had to resort to the DNA method. That is why, because of the large number and because of the very complex cases involved, where the population was quite similar to a degree, I'm talking about men of middle age or younger men, so in such cases it was very difficult to identify them, and that is why we had to use the DNA method which in 1998 or 1999 was introduced in the area as a valuable method and of sufficient quality to be able to carry out identifications. Then we began to apply that method routinely in the Ovcara case, but in -- even there we did not manage to resolve all the cases as we expected, so that even now there are some outstanding, unresolved identification cases. And that is why these methods were used in this way, we're talking about a large grave site.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that the DNA analysis is something that is relatively new. Does that mean that the application of the DNA analysis is new in Croatia, in Croatian medical circles and not in international medical circles? When was the DNA method of analysis discovered?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact year of that, but I know that relatively quickly we began to apply the method, the lab was established in 1994 in Zagreb, and it began to use this method of analysis, but it wasn't so perfected at that time, and with the passage of time, as a method, it became more and more perfect, faster, and yielded results of a greater quality. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to look at Exhibit 452. This is a new table. It was drafted by the forensic medicine institute. You provided explanations yesterday about this table in response to questions from the Chamber, and this table provides a break-down of identified remains according to the classic method. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about establishing the identity using the classic method you attached a lot of value to documents, if the documents had any names on them?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were important in the sense that such a document immediately provides some name. Then of course it needs to be checked and double-checked in order to be able to carry out a correct identification. But that is the initial step.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So a name and remains put together does not automatically mean that the identity of the remains is established?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In how many cases -- excuse me. In how many cases was the identity of remains established on the basis of documents? I counted and I established that in 41 cases the identity out of 93 persons, because we have, would you agree with me, 93 persons whose identity was established in the classic way?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In 41 cases the identity was established using documents. You then also cite a number of other parameters on the basis of which identity was established, of which the most frequent one, and that is in 20 cases, is a combination of such parameters. Doctor, can you tell me what that means, combination of two parameters, three parameters, all kinds of parameters?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about a combination as the main element for identification, what we mean are several parameters, a number of parameters. Of course we're always happy if, in the case of a combination, we have many parameters. General ones, height, age, sex and so on. And then those that have to do with clothes, documents, teeth and so on. The more parameters we have, the simpler it is to make an identification, and in that case combination is the correct term. If we have a combination of a small number of parameters, then they have to be very convincing. So a convincing parameter would not only be a document, we would also need to have a dental analysis, accompanied photographs, or documents indicating old fractures, braces, and other things. So in such cases a smaller number of parameters which are convincing can also be used for positive identification. So if we have a number of such parameters, a small number of them, but they are reliable, they are specific, they are strong evidence, then we can take that as being sufficient. Of course, all of that depends on the approval of the relatives, relatives or the family always has to accept an identification in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. So that means when you put down "combination" in the table, since it was not indicated what sort of a combination and which parameters are involved in each case, we cannot rule out that in all of the 20 cases or in a number of the 20 cases personal documents were one of the parameters in order to make the identification?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is always so. We always consider several parameters.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you are not ruling out the possibility that this number of 41 persons whose identity was established on the basis of documents could also be an even larger number, because of an as yet unestablished number of combination factors used to identify persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Because a document, if it's a reliable document, is quite overpowering evidence and we indicate it as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand the combination to mean a combination of all possible parameters, including documents.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, let me clarify it once again. If we have a document and other parameters, then the document will be emphasised, and that will be noted as the chief parameter used for identification. If we have other elements without documents, then we can have a combination, unless there is something that can be particularly convincing, which could be the dental history, tattoos or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, Doctor, can we say that when you are making autopsy reports, when you are carrying out identifications, is it common to indicate where documents were found, or the items that are being linked to certain -- a certain set of mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone who performs an autopsy in their report should emphasise or note down where any objects were found. Was it found in a pocket or next to the body, with the body, or something to that effect. It is necessary to write down where any item or document was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is 12.30. I don't know if it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. We will now adjourn for -- until a quarter to 2.00. So we will reconvene at a quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, let us now continue, please. Let us consider these identification issues and all the circumstances surrounding this work. Yesterday you testified in chief that the work of international experts, especially their work on autopsies, was correct or in keeping with the rules. That is page 44 of yesterday's transcript. No more and no less. You described their work as in keeping with the rules. You also say that their autopsies created a number of problems in your work at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These problems that you referred to yesterday were reflected in the fact that you did not have sufficient photographs, sufficient parameters, sufficient detail such as is normally obtained during an autopsy. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Primarily I had in mind good, solid photographs that we could use. Photographs of details that were described but not photographed sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This assertion to the effect that omissions may have been made during these autopsies, did possible omissions affect the identification of any remaining bodies or did this only affect the duration of the identification process itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this only affected the duration of the entire process. The process as a result became relatively slow. Ultimately, however, each body was identified in such a way as to make sure that both we and the families felt the ID thus achieved was reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Domazet, asked you a number of questions to do with the identification process, Especially the stage at which relatives could either choose to sign an identity certificate or refuse to sign a certificate. What I want to know now is from a purely medical point of view, if you have solid, reliable information on a person's identity, this person at this point no longer has a number but rather a name is assigned to a particular body. You've mentioned one such case. Would that be the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the classic method has been applied, however reliable it may be from a purely medical standpoint, we never pressed for this sort of result to be accepted under any conditions. We never considered the case closed, in purely medical terms. If there was a 99.9 per cent identification, an identification that confirmed our suspicions or theories, then we would normally accept this as a positive ID, even in cases where the family refused to sign the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me then that in these cases from a purely medical standpoint, a victim has been identified, but from a legal standpoint this person remains anonymous, as it were, an unknown person?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true when DNA analysis is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if the family refused to sign a certificate like that for any reason at all, there can be no death certificate issued. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. No death certificate, no burial.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you can't have an excerpt from the death register issued. I'm not sure if that book is still called the same in Croatian as it used to be?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name remains the same, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke yesterday about erroneous entry of information over the years. We had yet another table, one of the many that we have been dealing with. This is Exhibit 461, and it's at tab 2, for your reference, Mr. Strinovic. You confirmed yesterday that this table was compiled by the OTP. Neither you nor your office were actually involved in the production of this table, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. We did provide some of the information that went towards the making of this table.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Am I right in concluding that all the questionnaires printed by the government of the Republic of Croatia and the Commission for Detained and Missing Persons, all the questionnaires in relation to missing persons from the Vukovar Hospital, allegedly, were submitted to the OTP at their request?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about antemortal information or which other questionnaires or forms do you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With the Chamber's permission I will show you exactly what I mean. These are questionnaires or forms that we as participants in this trial, have received from the OTP. It reads "Government of the Republic of Croatia," you have the coat of arms right there, "Commission for Detained and Missing Persons." This is a standard form or questionnaire excising 11 pages. Can the usher please assist me with this. I wish to show the witness these forms. There is a name on it, please don't mention the name, just have a look and tell me if you recognise the standard form that appears to be used here. Mr. Strinovic, are you familiar with this sort of form or questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I am. This is the kind of form that we refer to as antemortem information. This is used from the day a person goes missing officially. This form is printed and then information is gathered in relation to all the missing persons in Croatia, and the same applied to the case of the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who exactly was entitled to report a certain person missing or to report a suspicion that a person had gone missing or had been detained?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a question for the Red Cross or for someone working with the office for detained and missing persons. I can't be positive about this. The nearest and dearest, the closest relatives, I should assume, but I can't provide you with a legal answer that would be well-founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I showed you this document, I asked you whether you knew about these forms and questionnaires being submitted to the OTP at their behest. Or is this something that the Croatian government decided to do of their own accord, or perhaps the commission for detained and missing persons itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't positive about this, I don't know if I can answer your question. I could speculate, but the truth of the matter is I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't speculate. You don't know, fair enough. You also spoke about what specific type of information was available to your commission, which type of information may have been available to Dr. Milewski as she was compiling her own report and opinion. Can you confirm that the Commission for Detained and Missing Persons, or rather the government of Croatia, obtained complete autopsy reports and findings containing all the information processed by international experts?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I believe I have stated this a number of times so far during my testimony, we received all the information save for information related to the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would I therefore be right to conclude that in the Republic of Croatia at this point in time no one is in possession of complete documentation in relation to these people who, for all we know, were, in fact, Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whether anyone at all in Croatia was given full sets of documents on the cause of death. One thing I do know is that we were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Strinovic, briefly, I am not likely to be dwelling on this for too long, but let us look into a problem that we raised yesterday ascertaining the degree of accuracy of information entered right at the start, the questionnaires and forms of the commission for detained and missing persons and then leading all the way up to such information as date of birth, name and surname, mistaken identity, something along the lines of the questions that my learned friend was asking. This is about OVC-009. I'm referring to that particular body by way of an example, or as an illustration. All I'm saying is that allegedly missing persons from Vukovar Hospital, 264 of them, were cited in the annex to the indictment in our present case. Among the persons cited there, there are two names and I'll have to say their names, one is Ivan Oreski. For your information, right next to that person's name there is a plus sign, which means that no mortal remains were ever found or identified. This person is listed as someone who was born in 1950. The next name in the indictment is Vladislav, Oreski. According to the indictment the body was identified and the year of birth was 1967. A while ago I showed you the questionnaire or the form in relation to one of these persons. Ivan Oreski. If I could have the usher's assistance for a moment, please. I would like to run something up on e-court. It's a 65 ter document. The number is 837. The ERN number is, the B/C/S reference, 0102-3987. Have you got that, Mr. Strinovic, can you see that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since we seem to have page 1 of this form on the screen right now, can we please now go to the next page, and the ERN or the number is 1, and the last three digits of the ERN number are 988. Do you have that, Mr. Strinovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've just received word that the other members of our Defence teams don't have that on their screens. The witness, however, does. I'm not sure if you do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, if you look at number 2, there is the name, the name is Ivan, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 3, surname, Oreski, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 10, date of birth. The 12th of April, 1950, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at your table, a table that has already been admitted, and the Exhibit Number is 461, tab 2. Please go to page [as interpreted] 88. Have you found that page?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 88, OVC-088, the name right there is Vladislav Oreski, date of birth, the 12th of April, 1950. The next thing you can see, or rather at the far end, the last column, 1967.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how this came about? How it came about that we have two different persons, one identified and the other still on the list, but still not found or identified? How can it come about that their representative details are mixed up in this way, although their dates of birth are quite different?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't do that just based on this table. I would need to go back to the original report or the death certificate. And then perhaps I would be better able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please go back to a 65 ter document, and the number is 837. We had it on our screens a while ago. And please if we could go to page 3 of that particular document. We will just have to wait a while for this to come up. Next page. Next page, the last three digits, 990. Question number 20 and the corresponding answer, can we please try to zoom in on that. Mr. Strinovic, we're still dealing with that document in relation to Ivan Oreski. Can you please read question number 20?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "State all the information known in relation to the person in question following the person's forcible abduction, disappearance or capture."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is the question. Can you now please read the answer, the handwritten answer?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the 22nd of November, 1991, to the beginning of January, 1992, he was at the hospital in Sremska Kamenica, and then later --" and then it says turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed it does, but there is as an asterisk there, too, isn't there? And in brackets it says "turn the page, please," right??

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can the usher please turn the page for us. Can we please zoom out a little so that the witness may have a view of the entire page. Mr. Strinovic, do you agree with me that the next page, page 4, does not show a continuation of the previous entry, which we were led to expect would be there. In this case the person entering the information was Mila [phoen] Oreski, the wife, who signed page 11?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite obvious that there is no continuation of the previous text on this page. I assume the continuation would have been on the reverse of the -- of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely my assumption too. I would like to ask you this now: Have you ever seen this particular form before?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I've seen thousands of these. I would be hard put to tell you if I've seen this particular one or not. We had different kinds of information in these. We see here that the person went missing on the 20th of November, 1991. But I don't know whether I've seen this one before or not. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't remember if you took any steps to follow this information through, what is stated here in answer to question 20 of the questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, whenever a case was nearing identification, the questionnaire would be re-checked. But what was really important, whether it was a case of the classic method being used or DNA analysis, was that antemortal information, the information provided to us, was extremely useful for identifying a body and for trying to find out who the body belonged to. However, all the information entered there, not all the information there was relevant or decisive and this was probably one such case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is because Mr. Oreski's wife indicates that he was at the hospital. Mr. Oreski is still listed as one of the persons in the annex to our indictment, still listed as an unidentified person, that is the reason I'm asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 519.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at Exhibit 459 in tab 5. No, I apologise. I was looking at what we've already dealt with. I would kindly ask the usher to show us document 381 on the screen. This being the report being Dr. Milewski, page 48. This part concerns the mortal remains of case OVC-002.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction for the transcript, this is case OVC-112.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that on the screen in front of you, Mr. Strinovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to zoom in. Thank you. Mr. Strinovic, could you read out Dr. Milewski's opinion, as I have already stated in paragraph 10 of her statement to the OTP she stated that she went through all the autopsy findings. Could you read out what she stated in her opinion here as regards OVC-112?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states cause of death, unascertained, or unestablished.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next line, please, the modality of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now please see the autopsy finding, being Exhibit 462, if we could have it on the screen, page 521. ERN number 0056-0249. Mr. Strinovic, this is an example of the autopsy report such as the ones we received, "we" being the Defence, for all 200 remains. In the upper left corner you can see that this refers to OVC-112, being the same mortal remains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please see page 3 of this report? Could we please zoom in on the bottom part of the page? Thank you. Could you please read out what is stated here? We know that you can use the English language. Could you please read out the last four lines on this page?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As cause of death, gunshot wound to the head. Manner of death, homicide.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, Dr. Strinovic, that what is stated here as regards the cause of death and manner of death are quite different from what you yourself read out from Dr. Milewski's report. I'm sorry, I can't really see you because of the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before providing my answer, I have to clarify. This is an example I've tried to explain before. When trying to establish the cause of death with people or whose bodies spent a considerable number of years in the ground, doctor wrote in her report that the injuries may have been caused by a bullet or some other type of projectile, but she couldn't make up her mind because the skull was so fragmented that she couldn't reach a final conclusion as to the cause of trauma. Hence, she wrote down "unknown." She explained this massive trauma to the head. On the other side the person who carried out the autopsy, based on the same parameters and the same defects to the skull made his own conclusion. He wrote down homicide and gunshot wound. This is an example of a complex case in which two different people of same qualifications can interpret things differently. One would specify reason unknown, the other will say gunshot wound. The third person would say trauma that might include gunshot wound. Therefore it is difficult to be specific as to the cause of death. I understand both the person who carried out the autopsy and the doctor because they were uncertain as to the actual cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tapuskovic. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a moment, Your Honours, to prepare myself. Good afternoon to Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the witness. My name is Momcilo Bulatovic, one of the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. On behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence team I will put some questions to you and I will my best not to repeat my colleagues' questions so as not to waste any time. Mr. Strinovic, in your report that you were asked about by Ms. Tapuskovic, I saw your particulars there and some background facts. I was particularly interested in item 9 where it reads that you can repeat that you were the coordinator of the medical part of the team during exhumation and identification, meaning that you selected the teams for this work. Could you please explain what specifically was your job in the process of identification and your presence at Ovcara during exhumations and autopsies? What did you do specifically?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a pretty complex question, inviting several answers. You probably want to know about my general duties I had during the identification process, and then separately as regards Ovcara itself. As for the general part, work was organised in such a way that until 1995 the commission of which I was a member since 1991 was primarily tasked with gathering information. As of 1995 onwards the commission focused on locating mass graves, on exhuming and identifying bodies. When the exhumation process began the amount of work expanded. There were numerous locations, large numbers of mass graves, and a lot of work. We needed to organise and dispatch teams. We knew that in certain parts of Croatia there were forensic pathologists who carried out some work during the war, and based upon the request of the governmental office and on my proposal, they were included in those teams which worked in the field, both in exhumations and subsequent autopsies and identifications. A large number of cases, particularly those more complex ones, were treated at the forensic institute in Zagreb. I was there, together with my colleagues, and we did all the autopsies there. And then we were also tasked with identifying the bodies and getting in touch with families. Therefore, the medical segment was what I was involved with in the entire process of locating bodies and identifying them. I worked with other physicians and with the teams I mentioned. On the other hand, I myself participated and was present at exhumations, especially at the beginning, together with some of my other colleagues. The same goes with autopsies, a large portion of those were carried out by the institute's experts who also worked in the field in Petrinja, Kostajnica, and elsewhere. Some bodies were treated in situ, while others were treated at the institute. Therefore we can look at this in two ways one of being the task of organising the whole process and the other hand I did everything the other experts and physicians did. As regards Ovcara, was tasked with being a monitor at exhumations and autopsies. I wasn't constantly present at exhumations because there was another colleague who attended regularly, basically on a daily basis. Throughout the process of exhumations, there was always at least one physician present. When those bodies were then transferred to the institute, the autopsy procedure began carried out by international experts, and together with Professor Matasuic [phoen], who came at that time from Nis in Serbia, attended regularly. We would go to the room which was adjacent to our institute and we followed the autopsies. As regards establishing the cause of death and elements needed for identification, that was my duty. As regards the treatment or the examination of mortal remains. After that the same were handed over to the Croatian side, and then we began with the identification procedure, which was carried out at our institute. I worked on it together with my colleagues. We processed the data, we got in touch with the families, and carried out identifications. What couldn't have been resolved in the classical way, the Zagreb lab headed by Dr. Hubak carried out DNA tests and then again we would call in families who would then be given the DNA results, and that's the way the Ovcara operation was carried out up until today, because we still have some cases that are open and we will continue working on it. Therefore, this is, in brief, the entire explanation of all the duties I have had since the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in you attending the autopsies carried out at the institute in Zagreb. When you attended those autopsies did you have any role there? Could you offer suggestions to the international experts, could you provide comments? What was your role and that of Professor Ratasevic's [phoen], as both of you appears there in the same capacity, but representing two different sides?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As my role was explained to me, my role of a monitor was to observe, rather than suggest or demand that additional procedures be put in place. There was a team who did that, which did that, whereas Professor Ratasevic and I could only observe, be present during the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your previous professional career did you work on autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your previous career did you deal with autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have concluded my specialisation 26 years ago and I have been working as a forensic pathologist for at least 30 years and I must have carried out some 10.000 autopsies single-handedly. Beginning with 1991 and the beginning of the war we began seeing specific cases and since then I've been gathering experience on working with mortal remains of those killed during wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning your presence during the autopsies carried out by international experts, were you required by the Croatian government to submit a report of your remarks of what was done?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had no special meetings and no requests were made. I was simply present there to try and establish that they follow the rules of the profession, but the government never asked me to write a report as to how and what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As such an experienced expert, could you see anything that could point to the lack of expertise or that those experts did something that wasn't by the book? Or to the contrary, were you convinced that they did everything according to the rules of their profession?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see and follow during the autopsies, it was teamwork. It was carried out both by forensic pathologists, by pathologists, by dental experts, by anthropologists who had an important role to play. Therefore, everybody was treated by several experts, and what I was able to observe was that it was done in a fair, correct manner, because they paid due attention and applied the rules of the profession. What I did say earlier though, is that we found some data insufficient, and there I wanted to say that there may have been more photographs. Some things were more obvious and had -- had we had more photographs, the work would have been easier for us. Perhaps some of the photographs were not of good quality. And some of the findings were described in the reports, but we didn't have the photograph. With such a photograph the identification process would have been far easier. That was my remark when I tried to explain the quality of the procedure. But as for the autopsies themselves, that was done in a correct way. At least three experts checked every single body, and I had absolutely no objections as regards their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The international teams which carried out the autopsies, did they comprise all of the people they should have, anthropologists, radiologists, dental expert, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large team, which had rotations but there were always several experts present at any time. But there was always a radiologist, an anthropologist, a dental expert, meaning people from various areas and I had no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The participation of a radiologist is very important in such autopsies when trying to establish the cause of death. Can you remember whether X-rays were taken of all remains before the autopsies so that perhaps in such a way any metal objects could be located as being important for the final findings.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [as interpreted] As far as I know, diascopy was done, which is a radiological examination. Before a body would be put in a bag, this was done by a radiologist. They did so in each of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this diascopy or radiological examination, what can be found by using that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A radiological examination is done to try and establish whether there are any shades caused by metal objects that become visible on X-rays. It can be either a prothesis, be it in the mouth or on some other part of the body, perhaps an artificial hip or something else. Another thing that we are particularly interested in are bits of shrapnel or something else that would have been the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether such objects were indeed found, and if so, was that recorded and perhaps later those objects analysed if a bullet was found, what calibre it was, if there was a bit of shrapnel, what it originated from?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know a number of such shades appeared indicating the presence of metal objects. There was also the criminal police present there, or rather their experts who worked together with the other specialists. They took out those objects and sealed them off separately, and we were told that they were being taken to The Hague to the Tribunal. After that we didn't see those objects again. Soon after such objects were located, they were extracted and taken away and we couldn't use them anymore for any other research.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 69, line 3 of the transcript, my question was merged with the answer. I believe that needs to be separated. Somewhere where it states "as far as I know," in line 3. Or "as far as I know." That is already the beginning of the witnesses's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, after the autopsies were completed, were the bodies of those autopsied then handed over to the government of Croatia, were any additional autopsies done on these bodies, any additional examinations, was anything else done in terms of establishing information that was not contained in the protocols which you received until the autopsy reports were completed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the bodies were received those persons who were already likely recognised were identified. All the cases, those cases and later cases, in case relatives or -- provided some new information or anything new appeared which was not in the autopsy report, the body was re-examined. And as far as I know, when we received the remains, DNA samples were taken in the cases where we felt it was required. DNA samples were taken from teeth, usually it would be taken from two teeth, and also from the thigh bone, just above the knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You responded to a question by my colleague, Ms. Tapuskovic, about what you received along with the body in terms of documents. Did you receive any additional information, were any other documents added to the autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just as you said. We received the protocol, there was another page with the dental examination findings, which was not thoroughly done, so we made additional analysis of teeth, so we eventually had our own protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in response to an answer [as interpreted] of my colleague Ms. Tapuskovic when she showed you the form by the commission for missing and displaced persons, that you were talking about antemortal data?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The international experts who did the autopsies, did they have the same information at their disposal? Do you know if they received copies of such a report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did have access to some of these antemortem information sheets, and on the basis of that they could obtain about 56 names that were first in line for identification. Yes, they did have the antemortem information at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The identification process for these 56 persons, the commission of which you were a part of, the Commission for Missing and Detained Persons, did you also participate in the work done by the international medical staff?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they worked completely separately, they received the antemortem results and then based on their own work they reached their own conclusions independently in relation to those 56 persons. We didn't work jointly, we began to work on the day that they left. The mortal remains had been handed over to us, we received the protocols --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were present at the autopsies that were done at the institute in Zagreb, I would like to ask you the following: Were the autopsies carried out in the same order that they were dug up? Were they done in the same order as the numbers which you received the mortal remains were unearthed, they were given a number, then there was a classification according to some standard, some criterias. How did you decide which order you would process the bodies in?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there wasn't any kind of strict order in which the autopsies were carried out. It depended on the accessibility of the body bags; the order that the body bags were placed on the table was the order that was followed for the actual autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, would you please look in the collection of documents provided to you by the OTP, if you look at Exhibit 461, and that is tab number 2. Did you find that table?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at under number 2, OVC-002, Antun Mutvar. Now, there is a column with the heading "date." Do you see it at the top, it says the 15th of November, 1996 in that column. Have you found it? For Ovcara 002?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It states there 15th of November, 1996. According to the records that would be the date of the autopsy, would it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you look at the two dates above and below for Ovcara 1 and for Ovcara 3, I'm not going to mention the names. We have the date 7th of October, 1996 in both columns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us if Ovcara 2 at the beginning, that would be a body that was exhumed, why was the autopsy carried out on the 15th of November 1996 while the others bearing numbers 1 and 3 were autopsied on the 7th of October, 1996? Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really, I don't have an explanation, probably that was the order that the body bags came in. Why this was so, I really have no idea. I can't give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The table that we had the opportunity to see, the one that was drafted for the classic identification method --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- and that was exhibited as Exhibit 452, what I would like to look at is the section where it says, "Bandages, woundings." Do you remember that? This is the table by the university for medicine, the institute for forensic medicine. And you can see that now on your screen. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do have the table in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to look at the column for bandages and wounds. You talked about that at the Belgrade Ovcara trial on the 20th of April, 2005. Could you please clarify a little bit exactly what this column means and where was this information acquired from that is in this column?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column for bandages and wounds contains information from the autopsy protocols that we received, which contain a section on wounding or reason for hospitalisation. This was an entry or a section maintained by the international experts. So in case there were any bandages or wounds, it is recorded if there is something like that or not. The protocols that you saw contains such a section, and we simply copied that section in our data. And that particular section existed in each protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were examined at the Belgrade trial, the so-called Belgrade Ovcara on the 20th of April, 2005, on page 4 of the transcript of that date, explaining this, you said the following: "Bandages and wounds is separate there. In some cases there were bandages, but no other wounds were noted. All that was noted was that there was some bandages that were applied or there were wounds, in the sense that it was evident and that there was a prior injury or wound. Maybe there was some amputations, there were some fractures that had been stabilised or surgically treated." I must note that there are a lot of typos in the transcript the way it is, but I think that we do understand one another. Doctor, could you please clarify what you mean when you say here, "previous wounds, surgical treatment," and so on, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, let's deal with the bandages. When a bandage is mentioned in the autopsy protocol, we also entered that into our database. A bandage would have been applied where there was a wound or on top of a plaster-cast, or it could have been placed in a place where there was no wound. So these were all possibilities for the existence of the bandages. And then when we're talking about wounds, or injuries, it could be anything, it could be some sort of skin injury, it could be a bone injury, any kind of injury. It could be organ injuries in the abdominal cavities, any kind of organ injury. And this again was noted in the protocol under the reason for hospitalisation. So it was either an entry for a wound or a bandage. Both of them were in the same column. As I said, the reason for the existence of the bandage would have been possible to establish or not. I hope that this was a little bit clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now you have given me a new topic for thought, because you mentioned that perhaps sometimes there was a bandage there when there was no need for it, so what would be the motive for somebody placing a bandage when there was really no need for that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your long years of practice, did you ever come across a case where somebody had applied a bandage without any reason or need?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible for anybody to place a plaster-cast without its actual being needed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In case an X-ray is taken, would such X-ray films show places of old fractures or wounds?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would always be possible to establish the existence of a perhaps newer fracture. Sometimes it would be difficult to establish that in case we were talking about a very small bone or a very slight fracture. But in cases of fresh bone fractures, this would be something that would come up on an X-ray.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the autopsy reports you had the cause of death and all sorts of other information that was mentioned there. So what I would like to know is the following: Can an autopsy establish the age of -- or how old the wounds were that are noted in the autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about each single autopsy, especially if it is being carried out using elements for identification, then in case a fracture is found one tries to establish how long ago the fracture occurred. So it is possible to establish whether it is a fresh fracture or if it is a fracture that is already began to heal of several weeks' standing or if several years or some time has passed since the fracture occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From what I understand then, it is possible, if we're talking about bone injuries, but if we're talking about soft-tissue injuries, what about then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how I understood the question, that it related to bones. If we're talking about soft-tissue wounds, then we can only determine that depending on how well preserved the mortal remains are. If the soft tissue has already disintegrated, then our assessment would depend on what actually has been preserved of the body. If the soft tissue is preserved, then it's possible to establish things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If several injuries are found, is it possible to determine the order in which these wounds were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, the order in which the wounds were inflicted is a very delicate question, and it's very difficult to provide a definite assessment. There is also a question of the different intensity of the injury, also the distribution of injuries, and then in some cases it is possible to determine whether an injury was inflicted at the initial stages, at the beginning and the others then followed. But this is very difficult, especially in the cases of victims of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Still talking about wounds, now we're talking about gunshot wounds. Is it possible to establish what type of fire-arm was used when the wound as inflicted, and we're talking about bones now and soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's very difficult to answer your question precisely. We have several situations. If the projectile is found in the body, then matters are clear. If there is no projectile but only the damage or the injuries there, and if the injury is on soft tissue, then it will not really be of much help. If we have a bone injury, it depends on the type of bone which was injured. Some bones shatter in a regular way, and then you would have a regular, round hole, and then you could determine the size of the projectile on the basis of the size of the hole. And then you could go on to determine the type of weapon. Some bones fragment into a lot of pieces, and then it's very difficult to establish the instrument of injury. It is quite sure that major damage, as compared to cases where there is minor damage to bones as well, can then indicate the speed of the projectile, and then indirectly with give an indication of the calibre, because we know that there are slow projectiles that are linked to certain weapons, there are very fast-moving projectiles which we can then relate to a different kind of weapon. All of these things are possible to see on the body, to see on the wounds, and then based on all those factors you could come to some sort of assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned or we mentioned shrapnel here. Is it possible to establish, you're not an expert for that, but in the case where shrapnel is found on the body, on the depth of penetration and the size of the hole caused, is it possible to establish the distance from which the projectile was fired?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shrapnel is a very complex issue, because shrapnel is very different. It's not of regular shape like a projectile is. There are different sizes, different speeds of shrapnel. So, first of all, it's very hard to find shrapnel in the body. It can be detected by X-rays, which is how it is most often done. During autopsy, if they are irregularly shaped they are often embedded in the bone or a part of the body, so it's not easy to find such fragments. If we're talking about the distance in comparison to projectiles where we do have some sort of guide-lines in the case of shrapnel, this is almost impossible. They're of different sizes, they can be different velocity, some can create surface wounds, some can create deep wounds, some can completely go through the body and exit the body. So perhaps this would then depend on the parts of the body which it was found, and then it could be discovered by X-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about fire-arms, now we're talking about a specific situation. I know that this is theoretically possible, but what about this situation: Is it possible to establish the distance from which projectiles were fired from a fire-arm?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, every type of fire-arm, depending on its charge, has matter leaving the barrel. And this goes some way towards indicating the distance from which this was fired. If the charge is considerable, then the dispersion of flame or pellets can be quite large. With smaller weapons it can be very little, about 30 centimetres, perhaps the dispersion will not cover a large area. It is based on this dispersion rate that you can ascertain a possible distance. Everything past this point is very difficult to detect in terms of ascertaining a distance. Since at this point we're looking at bullets and projectiles that have their own typical distinctive features. It also depends on type of injury found, is it just a lesion, is it a contusion, but it's difficult to about specific distances, whether it was fired at close range or what I described as relatively close up, it is possible to ascertain this. The further you get from this point the more difficult it is for us as forensic experts to ascertain the distance. It might be several metres, it might be long-range, for all we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have several questions, several more questions about this, I won't take long, I hope, but this might be a convenient time for a break, based on what you suggested yesterday. If I am wrong, I could as well go on, if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: That's all right. We will have our break now for 20 minutes, so we will reconvene at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, there's one question about something else that now occurs to me. Do you know that at point during the autopsies any canals caused by bullets were found in any of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really answer that question. I would need to go back to the original report and have a look. I can't say off the bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We heard that some projectiles or bullets were found. Were any pellets found in any of the bodies exhumed from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you some questions about the X-ray technique. I've had a look during the break, and I want to clarify some things. When you have an X-ray of a body, can we see both new fractures and old fractures?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you use the normal X-ray you can see both old and new fractures. When you apply diascopy, which is a similar technique, but the image is less sharp, it's nearly impossible to see any old fractures. Diascopy is a different kind of technique. It is usually applied when you need to get an overall picture of the whole body, usually in search of small metal objects, possibly lodged inside the body. So, yes, and you have a regular X-ray you might see that, if you use the other technique, diascopy, it's virtually impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When I say old and new, what would normally be considered an old fracture?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One that's already healed. The bone has grown back, and because of this there is a tumescence that you might see in an X-ray image. This tumescence is what leads you believe there was a fracture in that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You have received -- you received certain documents you mentioned some projectiles. Have you ever received any reports, have you ever received any documents about the sort of bullets and projectiles that were found in terms of calibre, number, size, type of weapon, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never received any of those. I did point out at the outset that we were only given the sections that have to do with identification. Afterwards we received the cause of death section too, but not in relation to such information as you have just specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I want to go back to Exhibit 452 [Realtime transcript read in error "542"], it should be still on the screen. Not 542, 452. The table that you compiled. This is the column that I was interested in, bandages and wounds. You have explained about that already. You say that you entered information into this table based on the reports that you received at the time, and based on everything that was established during the autopsies, such as the existence of bandages?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there we go. Just a minute. We need to confer about the transcript, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Ovcara number 48? 48. The name is Mihajlo Zera, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Under bandages, wounds, we see the word "yes" is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This means that based on information from the autopsy report you established that bandages were found on this person, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Either that or wounds. One or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have Exhibit 462, page 212, placed on our screens. Thank you. 212 of Ovcara 1, number 48. That's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page. ERN 0055-9941. That is the page. We're back to Ovcara 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we're waiting, while we're waiting for my colleague to get what he has asked for, I would like to say something about page 81 of the transcript. The witness's answer, lines 7 through 10. The witness spoke about the documents he received. My learned friend asked him about projectiles and the witness said he received documents, autopsy reports, I suppose, in relation to only issues of identification, but later on he received the cause of death details too. The transcript, however, reflects that he got a section from the autopsy report, that is in reference to details referring to the cause of death. I think that is a misinterpretation. Maybe the witness could clarify this for us. I mean whether he received a section of the autopsy report in relation to the cause of death or a separate document at a later stage in relation to the cause of death for all the bodies that were found. I think that's probably a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Bulatovic, could you please clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour, to clarify this confusion, if it's a matter of poor interpretation. I asked Mr. Strinovic in relation to any projectiles or bullets that were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any findings as to the number of the projectile, the calibre, the type of weapon that was used to fire them, or the barrel type, since I suppose different kinds of barrels were being used through which these projectiles were fired. Answer that first, please, and then I'll ask you further questions in clarification?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the cause of death, can you please repeat what you got from whom and when. If you received anything at all, needless to say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we only received a list containing the cause of death details but not the reports in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this clarifies the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to our previous question, Mr. Strinovic. This is a part of an autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just zoom in a little? I'm having trouble seeing what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The very end of the -- the bottom of the page. Sir, can you look at the last two sentences, what does it say? Can you read that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "Record of injuries preceding fatal injuries." And it reads "none."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please turn the next page now, page 42. Do you see this page?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the part relating to therapy, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No signs of therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago when we looked at bandages and wounds, it said bandages or wounds. Now, if my understanding is correct, there is no signed of that anywhere in the record, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain how it came about that an entry was made to the effect that there was something based on the document that you were using and yet the document shows nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really hard put to do this. If you let me look at page 1 in its entirety, page 2, rather, perhaps I could say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, can we please bring back page 41, the previous page. I'm just using the last two digits, I'm talking about 0055-99941 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a little, please? Further down. Yes, based on this there appear to be no signs of injuries or bandages. I really don't know how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When we started discussing this subject a while ago about bandages and wounds, we said that there were cases where there were bandages yet no injuries or plaster-casts without injuries. We have some evidence about why this was done, and we'll be using that later on. What I want to know is this: If there is a bandage, if there is a plaster-cast, which is probably part of some medical therapy, and all of this because there is an injury, after an autopsy is performed can an old injury be seen, be established, and can the cause for this sort of therapy be established?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the condition of the body. How advanced the changes were to the body. If we're talking about wounds, this depends on the degree of preservation of bones and soft tissue. If there is none of that, even once a bandage has been removed, you still won't know. If there is a bone injury, and once a was or a bandage is removed, one should be able to see traces of an injury there, and this would indicate what the original reason was for placing a bandage or a plaster-cast there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Given a situation like that, there is a bandage, there is a plaster-cast, you have an autopsy, these are removed, the soft tissue is gone underneath. Would this be clearly indicated in an autopsy report, no tissue, therefore it is impossible to ascertain whether there was an injury or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have expected that, and that's what an expert should record. No tissue, therefore no cause for bandage or cast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What if the report says that an examination has been carried out and no injury has been found underneath the cast, there is no visible injury to the soft tissue or the bone. Does that mean that the soft tissue was there, but whoever performed the autopsy found no traces of an injury, the assumption being if he had found anything he would have recorded it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would tend to agree with that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would not like to further tire you with this, but there are 41 different reports. If you'd like me to, we can do a blow-by-blow analysis and go into each and every one of these to see whether they tally with what we have just agreed on. There is a bandage, there is a plaster-cast, an examination has been carried out by a variety of international experts. It has been unequivocally ascertained that there was no injury underneath to the soft tissue or the bone. Mr. Strinovic, can we then agree that in at least 41 different cases, and that's what I'm talking about right now, the situation that was found was this: There was a bandage and a plaster-cast that were applied although there was no obvious medical reason for that to be done?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure. I didn't look at it like that, but in theory I do agree with you, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question, Mr. Strinovic. Something I've asked you before, and you partially answered this. I have a different reason for asking this question now. You used reports or parts of autopsy reports, later you had these reports on the cause of death, which you received. When you were using these, were you not, in fact, convinced that in keeping with what you told us, you monitored the procedure, and you believed the procedure to have been carried out in a perfectly professional way, and there was nothing to cause you any misgivings about the accuracy of those reports and the way information was recorded?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I monitored the procedure; it took over two months. I monitored the work of the experts there, and there was nothing to cause me any misgivings about the professional standards of their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, Your Honours, there is something that I need to confer with my learned friend about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So much for the bandages. Let me ask you something else. What about how old the injuries were, was it possible to ascertain that during an autopsy, be it soft tissue or bone? I have asked you about that, but I don't think it was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is an injury to the bone, you can tell how old it is. So this is normally recorded, old or fresh. When you have an autopsy you do see this normally, and that sort of information is recorded as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at all the reports for all the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at the type of injuries, the types of injuries that were recorded in these just over 200 cases?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about injuries that had nothing to do with the cause of death, in that case your answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: Can you tell me the various types of injuries that had nothing do, that were unrelated to the cause of death, the type and degree of those injuries as well as what the injuries were to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say off the cuff like this, there were plenty of those. Again you would need to have a table or a special report which would make it possible for me to specify what the injuries were. The ones that had to do with wounds, but not necessarily with the cause of death. The long and the short of it is I can't say off the bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any sort of information while identifying these bodies, you were monitoring these autopsies performed by foreign medical experts. Did you, or indeed did they have any medical files where admission or discharge from the Vukovar Hospital were recorded? Did you have the admission and discharge sheets?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
