utterances.text: Now that you've asked me this, this was one of the main problems, one of the crucial problems when identifying bodies for us. The fact that most of the documentation was not available to us. Case histories, X-rays, things that would normally have been found in a hospital. But these weren't available to us. We did not have the hospital's original files. We did have other documents relating to old injuries in some cases which proved helpful when identifying a given body. But the kind of files that you are referring to, this would have been extremely useful, this would have been even necessary, unfortunately we weren't given those at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your recollection, can you tell me if these injuries, those not related to the cause of death, but those that were recorded in the reports, would these injuries have required long-term medical treatment or long-term hospital treatment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say definitely, but there were all kinds of injuries, amputations, injuries requiring surgery. Were I to go any further than this, I would need to go back to the original sources or to the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness. Mr. Strinovic thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, I think you will be leaving us today, which I think will probably be quite pleasing for you. Doctor, perhaps I would like to show you an autopsy report which we have been discussing and the one I would ask to be called up would be Exhibit 462, and it's in relation to Ovcara victim number 48, please. And it's at e-court page 213. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, when we look at this report on Ovcara 48, you mentioned to my learned friend that there was no evidence of recent injuries or hospitalisation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we look at the top of the report we can see that there was an old fracture on the upper third of the left tibia. And if you can just remind us, what is the tibia, which bone is that in layman's terms?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an old fracture. It's the shin bone. We have the tibia fibula, that's one bone, and that's the thicker bone on the inside of the shin, it actually runs from the whole length of the lower leg, from your knee down to your foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the list that your office produced as to the main identifying features of the individuals, in relation to Ovcara victim 48, you stated that bandages and wounds were -- bandages or wounds were located on this person's body. Would this old injury account for that notation in the chart, or is it simply a mistake? If you can't say, just say.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the table, if you look at the columns, the categories, there is nothing else that looks like this. Therefore, an old injury, an old wound might be taken into account. For that reason, because the only category you have there is bandages and wounds, you could take into account an old injury like that, and that would be the reason behind this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now look at Exhibit 457, please. This is at tab 4 in your folder. And it relates to the general statistics in relation to the cause of death from the information that you were given. But more particularly I would like to refer you to the notation as to how many of the people of 200 exhumed were previously wounded. Now, in that chart you list 88 -- or is it 86 people that were previously wounded. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, if I can just refer you to Dr. Milewski's report, and perhaps I'll read it out, just so that we can speed things up a little. And this is Exhibit 381, and the ERN number is 0294-2944. In her report she states that in relation to part C, evidence of medical therapeutics, 55 per cent of the 200 individuals are described as having evidence of hospitalisation in the form of hospital clothing, evidence of treatment with or without underlying observable injury, or a combination of the above. Based on Dr. Milewski's conclusion, that would mean that 110 of the 200 people that were exhumed from Ovcara had some sort of evidence of hospitalisation, whether it be an injury or not. Now, if I can refer you back to the figure that you have in your chart of 88 previously wounded, obviously that's a different figure to that of Dr. Milewski. However, in Dr. Milewski's report she talks about other evidence of hospitalisation other than woundings. My question for you is, in relation to the 88 previously wounded figure that you determined, of that 88, would that include only evidence of individuals having bandages or some other hospitalisation, evidence without -- without including injuries? That's a long question, but if you can answer that.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke about the injured persons at Ovcara we received that kind of information from the reports. The reports indicated the existence of any injuries or previous treatment, medical treatment of those injuries. When this was ascertained at an autopsy, then it would be clearly stated that a given injury was not the cause of death, and had been treated. Those are the injuries under 86. We see that the lady doctor provided a slightly different figure. Now again we have this problem related to which criteria we decide to adopt, about whether someone was a patient of the hospital or not. Somebody might be wearing their pyjamas, for all I know, with no injuries at all, but he might be considered a patient. So this is another category, and I find that perfectly understandable, that in cases like this and also when assessing who was a patient and who wasn't, who was injured and who wasn't, there might be discrepancies precisely for this reason because the criteria applied is slightly different. Everyone tends to have a different view of what it means to be a hospital patient. All those wearing pyjamas, do they all qualify as patients? Or do you need something else to be considered a hospital patient, something over and above your pyjamas, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so just to conclude on this point, what criteria did you use to come up with the figure of 88 previously wounded individuals?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we aimed at persons who had indications of injuries, something that indicated that indeed it was a wounded person, and not just another patient in his pyjamas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would that exclude individuals that were exhumed that only had bandages or casts, but no other evidence of a wounding or an injury? Does that exclude that group or does it include that group?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the cases with bandages and casts were put inside the wounding or the wounded category.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so that's included in the figure of your 88; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But in any event, would the final determination be obtained from the autopsy reports themselves?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We could go through the documentation, and again try to establish the criteria to determine the precise numbers of those with bone injuries or injuries to some other parts of the body and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we can look at Exhibit 453 [sic]. Now, this is the chart that's at your tab 2, I believe. And this relates to the exhibit that was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor in conjunction with the material that your office provided us in relation to positive identifications and dates of birth. If I can turn your mind to page 6 where we were discussing with my learned friend Ovcara victim number 88, Vladislav Oreski. Now, in the missing persons report that was in relation to this individual that was shown to you, the date of birth was, as appears, the 12th of April, 1950. And also if we look at the date of birth for Mr. Oreski here in column number 4, the date of birth is also the 12th of April, 1950. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that that date has come from the exhibit that was tendered through you in the Milosevic case in 2003, which we've tendered here today, or yesterday. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Therefore, in relation to the date of birth that appears in the annex of the indictment, 1967, or the year of birth, which is different to that of 1950, on the documents that you have got, which date of birth or year of birth would you say was more correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the more correct one is the 12th of April, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in that sense it's an administrative error in relation to the annex. Would you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Strinovic, you will be pleased to hear that this brings your evidence to an end.
